overview: Nothronychus mckinleyi was the first therizinosaur described from North America, discovered in the Moreno Hill Formation of New Mexico (~91 Ma) and described in 2001. Its discovery filled a major gap: before Nothronychus, therizinosaurs were known only from Asia, and this North American representative confirmed that the group had dispersed across the Bering land connection during the Cretaceous.

Like all therizinosaurs, Nothronychus was a herbivorous theropod with a broad pelvis, leaf-shaped teeth, long arms with large claws and an overall body plan suited to browsing high vegetation. A second species, N. graffami, was described in 2009 from slightly different Utah strata.

fossilSites.name: Moreno Hill Formation
fossilSites.note: Turonian continental deposits with the Nothronychus mckinleyi holotype — the first North American therizinosaur.

fossilSites.name: Tropic Shale / Straight Cliffs Formation
fossilSites.note: Turonian marine-margin deposits with Nothronychus graffami — unusually, preserved in near-shore marine sediments.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: James Kirkland and Douglas Wolfe described Nothronychus mckinleyi from material recovered during road construction in New Mexico. The species name honours William McKinley; the genus name means "sloth claw." A second species from Utah was found in marine Cretaceous deposits — an unusual context suggesting the animal was washed offshore after death.

articles.title: North American therizinosaurs
articles.body: Nothronychus and the later-described Falcarius (from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah, ~125 Ma) document that therizinosaurs entered North America during the Cretaceous, probably from Asia via Beringia. Falcarius, earlier in time, shows more carnivorous-grade features than Nothronychus, suggesting the group was still transitioning toward herbivory when it arrived.

articles.title: Herbivory adaptations
articles.body: Nothronychus shows the full therizinosaur suite of herbivory adaptations: broad pelvis, opisthopubic configuration (pubis pointing backward, convergent with ornithischians), leaf-shaped dentition and expanded gut capacity. The arms were long with large curved claws, consistent with pulling down branches. Its forelimb proportions suggest browsing at different heights from contemporaneous sauropods in the same region.

fossilRecord.formations: Moreno Hill Formation, New Mexico, USA
fossilRecord.material: Partial skeletal material including vertebrae, pelvis and limb bones.
fossilRecord.paleo: Late Cretaceous of the southwestern United States, in a coastal plain setting near the Western Interior Seaway.
fossilRecord.evidence: The large manual claws and herbivorous theropod proportions confirm its therizinosaur identity as the first North American member of the group.

record.description: Nothronychus was a derived therizinosaur from the Turonian of the western United States, represented by two species known from partial postcranial skeletons; N. graffami also preserves more complete axial and girdle anatomy.
facts: Large manual claws, a broad pelvis and leaf-shaped teeth support a specialised herbivorous or omnivorous theropod body plan.
Feathers are likely by phylogenetic bracketing but are not directly preserved with the named skeletons.

review.ageReviewNote: Both named species are Turonian, around 93-90 Ma; the genus is not limited to a single 91 Ma point.

sources.citation: Hedrick et al. (2015), The Slothful Claw: Osteology and Taphonomy of Nothronychus mckinleyi and N. graffami
Zanno et al. (2009), Nothronychus graffami anatomy

residualUncertainty: Species-level differences and exact diet remain open.
Cranial anatomy and integument are incomplete.

evidence.material: Two partial skeletons representing two species, with extensive axial and appendicular material but limited skull remains.
evidence.formations: Moreno Hill Formation, New Mexico, and Tropic Shale, Utah, USA.
evidence.confidenceLimit: Exact skull shape, feather distribution and precise food are not directly preserved.
evidence.summary: Nothronychus was a derived therizinosaur from the Turonian of the western United States, represented by two species known from partial postcranial skeletons; N. graffami also preserves more complete axial and girdle anatomy.
